lesson.title: When Wants Collide: The Psychology of Motivational Conflict
lesson.summary: Motivational conflict occurs when a person is pulled by two or more incompatible goals at the same time, classically sorted into approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, and approach-avoidance conflicts, each with its own typical psychological signature.
lesson.body:
Drive-reduction theory generally treats one drive at a time, hunger pushes toward eating, fatigue pushes toward rest. Real life is rarely so tidy, multiple drives and goals are often active simultaneously, and satisfying one can interfere with satisfying another. Motivational conflict is the study of exactly this collision, of what happens psychologically when two or more motivations cannot both be fully satisfied at once.

The mildest and generally least distressing type is approach-approach conflict, choosing between two desirable options, such as deciding between two genuinely appealing job offers. Because both outcomes are attractive, this kind of conflict is usually resolved relatively comfortably, though the process of choosing can still involve some hesitation as the options are weighed against each other.

Avoidance-avoidance conflict sits at the opposite end, choosing between two undesirable options, such as having to either complete an unpleasant task or accept an unpleasant consequence for not doing it. This type tends to be the most stressful of the three, since there is no comfortable outcome available, and it can produce noticeable hesitation, procrastination, or attempts to escape the situation altogether rather than choosing either unwanted option.

Approach-avoidance conflict, a single goal or situation that carries both appealing and unappealing features at once, such as wanting a promotion that comes with more prestige but also more stress and less personal time, is the type that has drawn the most extensive research attention. A useful, though simplified, way to think about it is that as a person gets physically or psychologically closer to such a goal, the pull to avoid its downsides tends to intensify faster than the pull to approach its benefits, which helps explain why people often hesitate or waver right at the point of committing to a decision that looked appealing from a distance.

Many real decisions combine these patterns into what is sometimes called a double approach-avoidance conflict, where each of two or more options carries its own mix of pros and cons, choosing between two colleges, each with attractive and unattractive features, is a common example. Whatever the specific combination, motivational conflict is a reminder that behavior is rarely driven by a single clean motive, it usually reflects several competing pulls being weighed, consciously or not, against each other.
